claim: In mice, spared nerve injury replicates symptoms of human neuropathic pain.
source: In mice, spared nerve injury replicates symptoms of human neuropathic pain and induces upregulation of many genes in somatosensory neurons.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Spared nerve injury induces upregulation of many genes in somatosensory neurons.
source: In mice, spared nerve injury replicates symptoms of human neuropathic pain and induces upregulation of many genes in somatosensory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript and is a known phenomenon in the field.

claim: Uninjured neurons were unaffected by transection of major nerve branches.
source: Uninjured neurons were unaffected by transection of major nerve branches, segregating into many different classes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the single-nucleus transcriptomic data showing that uninjured neurons maintain their normal classification patterns after IOT.

claim: Uninjured neurons segregate into many different classes.
source: Uninjured neurons were unaffected by transection of major nerve branches, segregating into many different classes.
evidence: This is shown in the clustering analysis of sn-RNA sequencing data presented in the figures.

claim: Axotomy rapidly transformed damaged neurons into just two new and closely-related classes.
source: In marked contrast, axotomy rapidly transformed damaged neurons into just two new and closely-related classes where almost all original identity was lost.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sn-RNA sequencing data showing I1 and I2 clusters appearing after injury.

claim: Almost all original identity was lost in damaged neurons after axotomy.
source: In marked contrast, axotomy rapidly transformed damaged neurons into just two new and closely-related classes where almost all original identity was lost.
evidence: This is supported by the transcriptomic analysis showing downregulation of class-specific markers and clustering analysis excluding injury-related genes.

claim: Sensory neurons adopted the injury-induced transcriptomic state following various minor peripheral injuries.
source: Remarkably, sensory neurons also adopted this transcriptomic state following various minor peripheral injuries.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ISH and sn-RNA sequencing data from facial injury and scratch lesion models.

claim: The injury-induced transformation was reversible.
source: By genetically marking injured neurons, we showed that the injury-induced transformation was reversible, with damaged cells slowly reacquiring normal gene expression profiles.
evidence: This is demonstrated using the Atf3-IRES-Cre mouse line with viral labeling showing tdTomato-positive, Atf3-negative neurons over time.

claim: Damaged cells slowly reacquire normal gene expression profiles.
source: By genetically marking injured neurons, we showed that the injury-induced transformation was reversible, with damaged cells slowly reacquiring normal gene expression profiles.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic marking experiments and the re-expression of genes like Calca and Scn10a in recovered neurons.

claim: Transcriptomic plasticity was previously thought of as a driver of chronic pain.
source: Thus, our data expose transcriptomic plasticity, previously thought of as a driver of chronic pain, as a programed response to many types of injury and a potential mechanism for regulating sensation during wound healing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work linking gene expression changes to neuropathic pain.

claim: Transcriptomic plasticity is a programmed response to many types of injury.
source: Thus, our data expose transcriptomic plasticity, previously thought of as a driver of chronic pain, as a programed response to many types of injury and a potential mechanism for regulating sensation during wound healing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the similarity of transcriptomic changes across different injury models (IOT, facial injury, scratch lesions).

claim: Transcriptomic plasticity is a potential mechanism for regulating sensation during wound healing.
source: Thus, our data expose transcriptomic plasticity, previously thought of as a driver of chronic pain, as a programed response to many types of injury and a potential mechanism for regulating sensation during wound healing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the injury response is reversible and occurs with minor injuries that do not cause chronic pain.

claim: Noxious stimuli activate nociceptors triggering spatially localized pain.
source: For example, noxious stimuli activate nociceptors triggering spatially localized pain that serves to inform both immediate responses and future avoidance of risky behavior (Basbaum et al., 2009; Julius, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Spatially localized pain serves to inform both immediate responses and future avoidance of risky behavior.
source: For example, noxious stimuli activate nociceptors triggering spatially localized pain that serves to inform both immediate responses and future avoidance of risky behavior (Basbaum et al., 2009; Julius, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Various types of nerve damage result in neuropathic pain in human subjects.
source: For example, in human subjects, various types of nerve damage result in neuropathic pain, which rather than providing essential information about the external environment greatly impacts quality of life (Basbaum et al., 2009; Colloca et al., 2017; Costigan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Neuropathic pain greatly impacts quality of life rather than providing essential information about the external environment.
source: For example, in human subjects, various types of nerve damage result in neuropathic pain, which rather than providing essential information about the external environment greatly impacts quality of life (Basbaum et al., 2009; Colloca et al., 2017; Costigan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Spared nerve injury is modeled in animals by crushing or cutting major branches of a peripheral nerve.
source: This type of pain is often modeled in animals by spared nerve injury (SNI) where major branches of a peripheral nerve are crushed or cut (Cobos et al., 2018; Costigan et al., 2009; Guan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: Lesion of the sciatic nerve results in the development of mechanical allodynia.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that such lesion of the sciatic nerve and partial infraorbital trigeminal nerve transection (IOT) result in the development of mechanical allodynia (where gentle touch elicits pain behavior) and cold sensitivity (Basbaum et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2016; Cobos et al., 2018; Guan et al., 2016; Hardt et al., 2019; Ito et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Partial infraorbital trigeminal nerve transection results in the development of mechanical allodynia.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that such lesion of the sciatic nerve and partial infraorbital trigeminal nerve transection (IOT) result in the development of mechanical allodynia (where gentle touch elicits pain behavior) and cold sensitivity (Basbaum et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2016; Cobos et al., 2018; Guan et al., 2016; Hardt et al., 2019; Ito et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Mechanical allodynia is a condition where gentle touch elicits pain behavior.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that such lesion of the sciatic nerve and partial infraorbital trigeminal nerve transection (IOT) result in the development of mechanical allodynia (where gentle touch elicits pain behavior) and cold sensitivity (Basbaum et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2016; Cobos et al., 2018; Guan et al., 2016; Hardt et al., 2019; Ito et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text with supporting citations.

claim: Nerve injury results in cold sensitivity.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that such lesion of the sciatic nerve and partial infraorbital trigeminal nerve transection (IOT) result in the development of mechanical allodynia (where gentle touch elicits pain behavior) and cold sensitivity (Basbaum et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2016; Cobos et al., 2018; Guan et al., 2016; Hardt et al., 2019; Ito et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: In human neuropathic pain, symptoms typically develop slowly over a period of days.
source: Just as in human neuropathic pain symptoms typically develop slowly, over a period of days, and then persist long-term.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Neuropathic pain symptoms persist long-term.
source: Just as in human neuropathic pain symptoms typically develop slowly, over a period of days, and then persist long-term.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: SNI causes upregulation of genes in response to injury.
source: One well-characterized effect of SNI is the upregulation of genes in response to injury (Cobos et al., 2018; Guan et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2019; Wlaschin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Injury-induced genes encode neuropeptides such as galanin, neuropeptide Y, and neurotensin.
source: These genes encode neuropeptides such as galanin (Gal), neuropeptide Y (Npy) and neurotensin (Nts), transcription control factors including activating transcription factor 3 (Atf3), SRY-Box11 (Sox11) and cytokines like colony stimulating factor 1 (Csf1) that are all expressed in injured neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the literature and confirmed by the data in this study.

claim: Injury-induced genes encode transcription control factors including Atf3 and Sox11.
source: These genes encode neuropeptides such as galanin (Gal), neuropeptide Y (Npy) and neurotensin (Nts), transcription control factors including activating transcription factor 3 (Atf3), SRY-Box11 (Sox11) and cytokines like colony stimulating factor 1 (Csf1) that are all expressed in injured neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the literature and confirmed by the data in this study.

claim: Injury-induced genes encode cytokines like colony stimulating factor 1.
source: These genes encode neuropeptides such as galanin (Gal), neuropeptide Y (Npy) and neurotensin (Nts), transcription control factors including activating transcription factor 3 (Atf3), SRY-Box11 (Sox11) and cytokines like colony stimulating factor 1 (Csf1) that are all expressed in injured neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the literature and confirmed by the data in this study.

claim: Transcriptional changes after nerve injury are thought to be important for triggering neuropathic pain.
source: It is generally thought that these transcriptional changes are important for triggering neuropathic pain with recent work showing that upstream inhibition of this gene expression program attenuated pain (Wlaschin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Upstream inhibition of the injury-induced gene expression program attenuated pain.
source: It is generally thought that these transcriptional changes are important for triggering neuropathic pain with recent work showing that upstream inhibition of this gene expression program attenuated pain (Wlaschin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Upregulation of Csf1 expression after nerve injury has been genetically linked to development of chronic pain.
source: More specifically, upregulation of Csf1 expression after nerve injury has been genetically linked to development of chronic pain (Guan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The significance for most of the SNI induced gene expression changes remains to be determined.
source: However, the significance for most of the SNI induced gene expression changes remains to be determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Somatosensory neurons are diverse with wide-ranging conduction velocities.
source: Somatosensory neurons are diverse with wide-ranging conduction velocities, cell soma diameters, expression profiles of receptors, ion-channels and neuropeptides; they have select peripheral and central targets and also exhibit varied functional response profiles (Julius, 2013; Le Pichon and Chesler, 2014; Nguyen et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature.

claim: Somatosensory neurons have varied cell soma diameters.
source: Somatosensory neurons are diverse with wide-ranging conduction velocities, cell soma diameters, expression profiles of receptors, ion-channels and neuropeptides; they have select peripheral and central targets and also exhibit varied functional response profiles (Julius, 2013; Le Pichon and Chesler, 2014; Nguyen et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature.

claim: Somatosensory neurons have varied expression profiles of receptors, ion-channels and neuropeptides.
source: Somatosensory neurons are diverse with wide-ranging conduction velocities, cell soma diameters, expression profiles of receptors, ion-channels and neuropeptides; they have select peripheral and central targets and also exhibit varied functional response profiles (Julius, 2013; Le Pichon and Chesler, 2014; Nguyen et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature.

claim: Somatosensory neurons have select peripheral and central targets.
source: Somatosensory neurons are diverse with wide-ranging conduction velocities, cell soma diameters, expression profiles of receptors, ion-channels and neuropeptides; they have select peripheral and central targets and also exhibit varied functional response profiles (Julius, 2013; Le Pichon and Chesler, 2014; Nguyen et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature.

claim: Somatosensory neurons exhibit varied functional response profiles.
source: Somatosensory neurons are diverse with wide-ranging conduction velocities, cell soma diameters, expression profiles of receptors, ion-channels and neuropeptides; they have select peripheral and central targets and also exhibit varied functional response profiles (Julius, 2013; Le Pichon and Chesler, 2014; Nguyen et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature.

claim: Single nucleus-based RNA sequencing does not require cell purification.
source: We reasoned that transcriptomic analysis of nuclei (Lacar et al., 2016), which does not require cell purification (Figure 1a), might provide a less biased description of the neural complement of the trigeminal ganglion and used a targeted nuclear sequencing approach (Figure 1a) to selectively analyze sn-transcriptomes from more than 7500 neurons (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: More than 7500 neurons were analyzed using single nucleus sequencing.
source: We reasoned that transcriptomic analysis of nuclei (Lacar et al., 2016), which does not require cell purification (Figure 1a), might provide a less biased description of the neural complement of the trigeminal ganglion and used a targeted nuclear sequencing approach (Figure 1a) to selectively analyze sn-transcriptomes from more than 7500 neurons (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Major divisions between trigeminal neural-types characterized by single cell sequencing were segregated in the sn-analysis as distinct clusters.
source: Major divisions between trigeminal neural-types that had been characterized by single cell sequencing (Nguyen et al., 2017) were segregated in the sn-analysis as distinct clusters expressing diagnostic markers (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the current sn-RNA sequencing data with previous single-cell data, as shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Data from nuclei more closely matched the neural composition of the trigeminal ganglion than single cell data.
source: Data from the nuclei much more closely matched the neural composition of the trigeminal ganglion (Nguyen et al., 2017) and were dominated by S100b-expressing large diameter neurons that now could be divided into several new sub-classes (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sn-RNA sequencing data showing better representation of large diameter neurons.

claim: Nuclear RNA sequencing data were dominated by S100b-expressing large diameter neurons.
source: Data from the nuclei much more closely matched the neural composition of the trigeminal ganglion (Nguyen et al., 2017) and were dominated by S100b-expressing large diameter neurons that now could be divided into several new sub-classes (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown in the clustering analysis in Figure 1c.

claim: S100b-expressing large diameter neurons could be divided into several new sub-classes.
source: Data from the nuclei much more closely matched the neural composition of the trigeminal ganglion (Nguyen et al., 2017) and were dominated by S100b-expressing large diameter neurons that now could be divided into several new sub-classes (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown in the clustering analysis in Figure 1c.

claim: Fos and Egr1 were prominent in earlier single cell analysis.
source: The benefit of using nuclear rather than cellular RNA sequencing and reduced handling was demonstrated by the accurate representation of immediate early genes like the proto-oncogene c-Fos (Fos) and early growth response protein 1 (Egr1) in the sn-data. Both genes were prominent in the earlier single cell analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a comparing single cell and sn-RNA sequencing data.

claim: In situ hybridization did not detect high level expression of Fos and Egr1 in a significant number of cells.
source: By contrast, in situ hybridization (ISH) did not detect at high level or a significant number of cells expressing these genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), which instead matched data from sn-sequencing.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b with ISH images.

claim: Atf3 and Gal expression in sn-sequencing corresponded to in situ hybridization results.
source: Importantly, genes that are thought to be markers of neural damage such as Atf3 and Gal also corresponded to in situ hybridization results in the nuclei-based dataset but were much more frequently detected in sequencing of isolated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing ISH and sequencing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atf3 and Gal were more frequently detected in sequencing of isolated cells than in sn-sequencing.
source: Importantly, genes that are thought to be markers of neural damage such as Atf3 and Gal also corresponded to in situ hybridization results in the nuclei-based dataset but were much more frequently detected in sequencing of isolated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing single cell and sn-RNA sequencing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two days after nerve transection precedes maximal injury-related changes in mechanical allodynia in most SNI models.
source: In most SNI models, this time-point precedes maximal injury-related changes in mechanical allodynia (Cobos et al., 2018; Hardt et al., 2019; Wlaschin et al., 2018) but already induces expression of injury-related markers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two days after nerve transection already induces expression of injury-related markers.
source: In most SNI models, this time-point precedes maximal injury-related changes in mechanical allodynia (Cobos et al., 2018; Hardt et al., 2019; Wlaschin et al., 2018) but already induces expression of injury-related markers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2 showing expression of injury markers at day 2.

claim: Most trigeminal neurons displayed a normal array of diverse gene expression profiles after IOT.
source: Indeed, most trigeminal neurons displayed a normal array of diverse gene expression profiles, clustering into classes (Figure 2a) corresponding to those seen in the uninjured control (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in the clustering analysis in Figure 2a.

claim: Very few damaged neurons expressing Atf3 were associated with standard trigeminal neural classes.
source: By contrast, very few damaged neurons expressing Atf3 were associated with these standard trigeminal neural classes and, instead, clustered together in two new related groups, I1 and I2 that were well separated from uninjured neurons in the UMap projection (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is shown in the clustering analysis in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Damaged neurons clustered together in two new related groups, I1 and I2.
source: By contrast, very few damaged neurons expressing Atf3 were associated with these standard trigeminal neural classes and, instead, clustered together in two new related groups, I1 and I2 that were well separated from uninjured neurons in the UMap projection (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is shown in the clustering analysis in Figure 2a,b.

claim: I1 and I2 were well separated from uninjured neurons in the UMap projection.
source: By contrast, very few damaged neurons expressing Atf3 were associated with these standard trigeminal neural classes and, instead, clustered together in two new related groups, I1 and I2 that were well separated from uninjured neurons in the UMap projection (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is shown in the UMap visualization in Figure 2a,b.

claim: I1 and I2 accounted for approximately 13.8% of sequenced neurons at day 2 after IOT.
source: In combination, I1 and I2 accounted for 635 of 4611 sequenced neurons (approx. 13.8%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing data.

claim: Injured neurons over-expressed a series of genes including many previously linked to nerve damage.
source: Transcriptome analysis revealed that the injured neurons over-expressed a series of genes (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) including many that have been previously linked to nerve damage (Table 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, and Table 1a with citations to previous work.

claim: Even without injury-related transcripts playing a role in clustering, Atf3-expressing neurons still grouped together as two related classes.
source: Remarkably, even without these injury-related transcripts playing a role, Atf3-expressing neurons still grouped together as two related classes and remained segregated from the uninjured trigeminal neural classes (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by re-clustering analysis excluding injury-related genes, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Atf3-expressing neurons remained segregated from uninjured trigeminal neural classes even when injury-related genes were excluded from clustering.
source: Remarkably, even without these injury-related transcripts playing a role, Atf3-expressing neurons still grouped together as two related classes and remained segregated from the uninjured trigeminal neural classes (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by re-clustering analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Trpv1, Tac1, Calca, Grik1 and Scn10a are normally expressed at high levels in significant numbers of trigeminal neurons.
source: The chosen genes, Trpv1, protachykinin 1 (Tac1), calcitonin gene-related peptide 1 (Calca), kainate one receptor (Grik1) and Scn10a are normally expressed at high levels in significant numbers of trigeminal neurons (Figure 2d,e upper panels).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 2d,e upper panels.

claim: Trpv1, Tac1, Calca, Grik1 and Scn10a were far less often present in Atf3-positive cells.
source: These genes were far less often present in Atf3-positive cells (Figure 2d,e, lower panels, see Supplementary file 1 for quantitation and statistical analysis).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 2d,e lower panels and quantified in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Atf3-positive cells expressing Trpv1, Tac1, Calca, Grik1 or Scn10a typically exhibited reduced signal intensity compared to surrounding uninjured neurons.
source: In addition, the few Atf3-positive cells expressing these transcripts typically exhibited reduced signal intensity when compared to the surrounding uninjured neurons (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 2d,e.

claim: Scn10a is expressed in nearly half of the trigeminal neurons.
source: Notably, for Scn10a, which is expressed in nearly half of the trigeminal neurons (Figure 1b, Figure 2e), this led to distinctive holes in its expression pattern across the regions of the ganglion where Atf3-positive neurons were strongly clustered (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b and Figure 2e.

claim: Within 2 days of injury there is upregulation of a shared set of injury markers.
source: Thus, in combination our data demonstrate that within 2 days of injury there is upregulation of a shared set of injury markers and strong downregulation of many genes that are normally prominent markers of the different trigeminal neural classes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transcriptomic and ISH data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Within 2 days of injury there is strong downregulation of many genes that are normally prominent markers of different trigeminal neural classes.
source: Thus, in combination our data demonstrate that within 2 days of injury there is upregulation of a shared set of injury markers and strong downregulation of many genes that are normally prominent markers of the different trigeminal neural classes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transcriptomic and ISH data presented in Figure 2.

claim: I1 neurons typically expressed markers that are normally prominent in larger diameter neurons involved in more discriminative types of sensation.
source: I1 neurons typically expressed markers including protocadherin 7 (Pcdh7), Piezo2, netrin G1 (Ntng1), microtubule associated protein 2 (Map2) and FAT atypical cadherin 2 (Fat3) that normally are prominent in larger diameter neurons involved in more discriminative types of sensation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A large subset of injured neurons still expressed Piezo2.
source: ISH confirmed that a large subset of injured neurons still expressed Piezo2 (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH image in Figure 2f.

claim: I2 neurons had an expression profile more related to nociceptors.
source: I2 neurons had an expression profile more related to nociceptors and instead expressed genes like tee-shirt homology domain 2 (Tshz2), regulator of G protein signaling 4 (Rgs4) and calcium voltage gated channel subunit alpha 1 c (Cacna1c) that are normally markers of smaller diameter neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gfra1 was primarily expressed in I1 neurons.
source: For example, GDNF-family receptor 1 (Gfra1) was primarily expressed in I1 neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The neuropeptide Gal was largely restricted to I2.
source: By contrast the neuropeptide Gal was largely restricted to I2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and selectively labeled just a subset of injured neurons in double label ISH (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2g.

claim: Axon-transection induces a remarkably consistent transcriptional transformation in diverse types of trigeminal neurons to produce an injured neural state retaining just vestiges of the gene expression patterns that distinguish classes of uninjured neurons.
source: Thus, taken together our data show that axon-transection induces a remarkably consistent transcriptional transformation in the diverse types of trigeminal neurons to produce an injured neural state retaining just vestiges of the gene expression patterns that distinguish classes of uninjured neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: Uninjured classes of trigeminal neuron were all distinguished in the co-clustering analysis and segregated from the injured neural classes.
source: As expected, uninjured classes of trigeminal neuron were all distinguished in this analysis and segregated from the injured neural classes (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is shown in the co-clustering analysis in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The most striking feature of the time-course analysis was the stability of the clustering across all time-points.
source: However, the most striking feature revealed by our analysis was the stability of the clustering, including all the uninjured clusters and the two classes of injured neurons (I1, I2) across the time-course (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c displaying data from different time-points.

claim: At 7 days after injury, approximately 13.4% of neurons grouped into I1 and I2.
source: At 7 days after injury, 539 from 4033 of total neurons (approx. 13.4%) grouped into I1 and I2, similar to the 13.8% observed at day 2.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing data.

claim: By 21 days post injury only 7.1% of neurons segregated into the injury-related clusters.
source: However, by 21 days post injury only 288 of 4046 neurons (7.1%) segregated into the injury-related clusters and 75 days after surgery this ratio had fallen further to 104 of 3634 neurons (approx 2.9%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing data.

claim: 75 days after surgery approximately 2.9% of neurons segregated into injury-related clusters.
source: However, by 21 days post injury only 288 of 4046 neurons (7.1%) segregated into the injury-related clusters and 75 days after surgery this ratio had fallen further to 104 of 3634 neurons (approx 2.9%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing data.

claim: There is a progressive loss of cells with injury-related transcriptomic features at longer times after injury.
source: Therefore, although the injury-related states are very long-lived, there is a progressive loss of cells with these transcriptomic features at longer times after injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreasing proportion of injured neurons over time shown in the data.

claim: The consistent clustering patterns rule out the possibility that injured or uninjured neurons slowly transition into new states during the timeframe from 2 to 75 days after injury.
source: The consistent clustering patterns of the individual timepoints in the UMap projection (Figure 3c) from 2 to 75 days after injury rule out the possibility that either injured or uninjured neurons slowly transition into new states during this timeframe.
evidence: This is inferred from the stable clustering patterns shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Lmo7 was rapidly upregulated but downregulated at later time-points after injury.
source: Examples include the Lim only domain protein 7 (Lmo7), which was rapidly upregulated but downregulated at later time-points and two injury-related neuropeptides Nts and Npy that were more slowly upregulated (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown in the gene expression analysis in Figure 3d.

claim: Nts and Npy were more slowly upregulated after injury.
source: Examples include the Lim only domain protein 7 (Lmo7), which was rapidly upregulated but downregulated at later time-points and two injury-related neuropeptides Nts and Npy that were more slowly upregulated (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown in the gene expression analysis in Figure 3d.

claim: Within 2 days of IOT, damaged neurons adopted a very stable injured state that was quite distinct from any undamaged class of trigeminal neurons.
source: However, the most significant conclusion from the time-course of transcriptomic changes following injury was that within 2 days of IOT, damaged neurons adopted a very stable injured state that was quite distinct from any undamaged class of trigeminal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the time-course data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Mechanical sensitization and tactile allodynia usually take a week or more to fully develop after nerve injury.
source: In contrast, mechanical sensitization and tactile allodynia usually take a week or more to fully develop after nerve injury (Cobos et al., 2018; Hardt et al., 2019; Wlaschin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Central processing of somatosensory input plays a major role in neuropathic pain.
source: Therefore, our results are consistent with recent data suggesting that central processing of somatosensory input plays a major role in this type of neuropathic pain (Guan et al., 2016; Szczot et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the timing mismatch between transcriptomic changes and pain development, supported by citations.

claim: The presence of a small number of neurons with injury-related gene expression profiles in uninjured control animals suggested that the injured state might be induced without axotomy.
source: Indeed, the presence of a small number of neurons in uninjured control animals that exhibited these gene expression profiles (Figure 3c) suggested that the injured state might be induced without axotomy and led us to investigate if modest nerve damage could trigger the transformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of a few injured-state neurons in controls shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Sham IOT surgery involves a cut to the facial skin and blunt dissection of muscle to expose but not injure the nerve.
source: This surgery involves a cut to the facial skin and blunt dissection of muscle to expose but not injure the nerve and thus results in a localized but significant peripheral injury.
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: Sham IOT surgery results in a localized but significant peripheral injury.
source: This surgery involves a cut to the facial skin and blunt dissection of muscle to expose but not injure the nerve and thus results in a localized but significant peripheral injury.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the sham surgery.

claim: In mice subjected to sham IOT surgery, ISH consistently revealed a small number of Atf3 positive cells clustered together in the trigeminal ganglion.
source: In mice subjected to this surgery, ISH consistently revealed a small number of Atf3 positive cells that were clustered together in the trigeminal ganglion (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 4a.

claim: Atf3-positive cells after sham surgery expressed several genes that are normally upregulated after nerve injury including Sox11, Sema6a, Csf1 and Gal.
source: These cells expressed several genes that are normally upregulated after nerve injury including Sox11, Sema6a, Csf1 and Gal (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 4a.

claim: Minor facial injury and scratch lesions induced Atf3-positive neurons.
source: To do this, we used a minor facial injury model (a series of extensive skin incisions to the facial area that just cut through the dermis) and examined mice that exhibited a chronic itch-like phenotype where scratching had produced obvious shallow skin lesions in the head and neck area (scratch lesions). In both cases, Atf3-positive neurons were detected by ISH and just as in the case of sham surgery these cells also expressed other markers of nerve injury (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 4a.

claim: The same transcriptomic program is upregulated following various types of relatively minor peripheral injury as well as after transection of major branches of the trigeminal nerve.
source: Thus, it appears that the same transcriptomic program (Wlaschin et al., 2018) is upregulated following various types of relatively minor peripheral injury as well as after transection of major branches of the trigeminal nerve.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ISH data from multiple injury models shown in Figure 4.

claim: Minor peripheral injuries downregulated functionally significant genes in Atf3-positive neurons.
source: The three types of minor peripheral injury also downregulated functionally significant genes. Just as we showed after IOT (Figure 2), Atf3-positive neurons expressed only low levels of key genes including Scn10a, Calca, Tac1 and Trpv1 (Figure 4b), suggesting that the normal sensory function of these cells must be dramatically changed.
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 4b.

claim: The normal sensory function of injured cells must be dramatically changed.
source: The three types of minor peripheral injury also downregulated functionally significant genes. Just as we showed after IOT (Figure 2), Atf3-positive neurons expressed only low levels of key genes including Scn10a, Calca, Tac1 and Trpv1 (Figure 4b), suggesting that the normal sensory function of these cells must be dramatically changed.
evidence: This is inferred from the downregulation of key sensory genes shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Atf3-positive neurons from both minor injury models were grouped with I1 and I2 neurons from IOT mice in co-clustering analysis.
source: Remarkably, Atf3-positive neurons from both minor injury models were grouped with I1 and I2 neurons from IOT mice (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown in the co-clustering analysis in Figure 5b.

claim: In scratch lesion mice, most damaged neurons were in the I2 class.
source: There were small differences, for example, in scratch lesion mice, most damaged neurons were in the I2 class with several likely related to normal C3 neurons (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown in the clustering analysis in Figure 5b.

claim: Both minor injury models showed low-level upregulation of Gal in neurons outside the I1 and I2 classes.
source: One other difference that was evident for both minor injury models was low-level upregulation of Gal in neurons outside the I1 and I2 classes (Figure 5c) in keeping with ISH results (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c and Figure 4a.

claim: There is great similarity but not complete identity between the transcriptomic profiles of neurons damaged in peripheral injury models and after nerve transection.
source: However, these data and additional gene expression analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c and Figure 5—figure supplement 2) confirm great similarity but not complete identity between the transcriptomic profiles of neurons damaged in peripheral injury models and after nerve transection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: After facial cuts had healed, ISH localization anecdotally indicated decreased expression of injury-related transcripts.
source: Indeed, after facial cuts had healed, ISH localization anecdotally indicated decreased expression of injury-related transcripts.
evidence: This is an observation from ISH experiments.

claim: Three weeks after injury, a few Atf3-positive cells were still observed in the trigeminal ganglion.
source: Nonetheless, even three weeks after injury and thus long after healing of the skin, a few Atf3-positive cells were still observed in the trigeminal ganglion.
evidence: This is an observation from ISH experiments.

claim: Significant cell death after SNI has been well characterized.
source: However, in both cases it is equally possible that injured neurons progressively die, and indeed significant cell death after SNI has been well characterized (Himes and Tessler, 1989; Vestergaard et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Adult animals not subjected to nerve injury exhibited only very sparse expression of Atf3 and no detectable tdTomato in trigeminal neurons.
source: As expected, adult animals, not subjected to nerve injury exhibited only very sparse expression of Atf3 and no detectable tdTomato in trigeminal neurons (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 6a.

claim: After IOT, prominent labeling of trigeminal neurons with tdTomato was observed.
source: In contrast, after IOT, prominent labeling of trigeminal neurons with tdTomato was observed (Figure 6b–d).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 6b-d.

claim: The viral labeling strategy targets about 30-50% of trigeminal neurons.
source: Note that the viral labeling strategy targets about 30–50% of trigeminal neurons meaning that only a proportion of the Atf3-Cre neurons (green) activate tdTomato expression (red).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the efficiency of the viral labeling approach.

claim: The percentage of tdTomato-neurons that were Atf3-negative rose from 11.0 ± 5.3% at day-7 to 42.7 ± 14.7% at day-21.
source: Quantitation of data revealed that the percentage of tdTomato-neurons that were Atf3-negative rose from 11.0 ± 5.3% at day-7 to 42.7 ± 14.7% at day-21 (see Supplementary file 1 for details and statistics).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ISH experiments.

claim: The change in Atf3-negative tdTomato-positive neurons parallels the decrease in number of I1 and I2 neurons identified by sn-transcriptomics.
source: This change parallels the decrease in number of I1 and I2 neurons identified by sn-transcriptomics (Figure 3), demonstrating that even after IOT many of the damaged neurons recover rather than die.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the genetic marking data with the sequencing data from Figure 3.

claim: Even after IOT many of the damaged neurons recover rather than die.
source: This change parallels the decrease in number of I1 and I2 neurons identified by sn-transcriptomics (Figure 3), demonstrating that even after IOT many of the damaged neurons recover rather than die.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the genetic marking experiments showing Atf3-negative, tdTomato-positive neurons.

claim: Recovered neurons must reacquire a normal trigeminal neuron gene expression profile since no new classes of trigeminal neuron were detected in sn-analysis.
source: These cells must reacquire a normal trigeminal neuron gene expression profile since no new classes of trigeminal neuron were detected in corresponding sn-analysis (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of new clusters in the time-course analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Calca and Scn10a were very rarely co-expressed with Atf3.
source: For example, Calca and Scn10a were very rarely co-expressed with Atf3 (Figure 6 lower panels) but were detected in a large subset (approx. 40%, see Supplementary file 1 for quantitation and statistics) of the recovered neurons (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is shown in the ISH images in Figure 6 lower panels.

claim: Calca and Scn10a were detected in approximately 40% of recovered neurons.
source: For example, Calca and Scn10a were very rarely co-expressed with Atf3 (Figure 6 lower panels) but were detected in a large subset (approx. 40%, see Supplementary file 1 for quantitation and statistics) of the recovered neurons (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is quantified from the ISH data shown in Figure 6c,d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The residual traces of original neural class retained amongst damaged neurons make it most likely that neurons return to their own original transcriptional state after recovery from injury.
source: However, the residual traces of original neural class that were retained amongst damaged neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) make this the most likely scenario.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that I1 and I2 retain some markers of their original classes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A stereotyped injured neural state is induced not only by nerve transection but also by other far less significant types of trauma.
source: First, we demonstrated that a stereotyped injured neural state is not only induced by nerve transection but also by other far less significant types of trauma.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data from multiple injury models presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Minimal injury such as self-inflicted scratch lesions or cuts through the dermis induced a very similar change in neural gene-expression profile to nerve transection.
source: Minimal injury such as self-inflicted scratch lesions or cuts through the dermis but not deeper layers of the skin induced a very similar change in neural gene-expression profile to nerve transection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ISH and sn-RNA sequencing data from minor injury models shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Many of the genes that are upregulated by injury have roles in tissue remodeling, neural development, and axon guidance.
source: Second, many of the genes that are upregulated by injury have roles in tissue remodeling, neural development, and axon guidance (see Table 1a and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by GO-analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and gene annotations in Table 1a.

claim: Upregulated genes probably contribute to restoration of normal peripheral innervation of tissue during wound healing.
source: These genes probably contribute to restoration of normal peripheral innervation of tissue during wound healing (Shin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional roles of the upregulated genes and supported by a citation.

claim: The injury response involves downregulation of genes encoding receptors, ion channels and neuropeptides that normally play major roles in sensory detection and signaling.
source: Thirdly, the injury response involves downregulation of genes encoding receptors, ion channels and neuropeptides that normally play major roles in sensory detection and signaling (see Table 1b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transcriptomic and ISH data showing downregulation of sensory genes.

claim: Widespread transcriptomic silencing of functionally relevant molecules may help prevent damaged neurons from conveying aberrant sensory input to central targets.
source: We speculate that this widespread transcriptomic silencing of functionally relevant molecules may help prevent damaged neurons from conveying aberrant sensory input to central targets.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed downregulation of sensory genes.

claim: Genetic marking of damaged cells and sn-transcriptomic data show that the injury-induced state is transient and likely to be reversible.
source: Fourthly, genetic marking of damaged cells using a new Atf3-IRES-Cre line (Figure 5) and sn-transcriptomic data (Figures 1 and 2) show that the injury-induced state, although potentially long-lived, is transient and likely to be reversible.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the genetic marking experiments in Figure 6 and the time-course data in Figure 3.

claim: The transcriptomic transformation induced by axotomy is a standard response to many types of peripheral trauma probably serving as an important driver for restoration of sensation.
source: Thus, rather than simply being a predictor of morbidity after serious nerve damage, we surmise that the transcriptomic transformation induced by axotomy is in fact a standard response to many types of peripheral trauma probably serving as an important driver for restoration of sensation and providing a mechanism for modulating sensory input from sites of injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the data showing similar responses across injury types and reversibility.

claim: The transcriptomic transformation provides a mechanism for modulating sensory input from sites of injury.
source: Thus, rather than simply being a predictor of morbidity after serious nerve damage, we surmise that the transcriptomic transformation induced by axotomy is in fact a standard response to many types of peripheral trauma probably serving as an important driver for restoration of sensation and providing a mechanism for modulating sensory input from sites of injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the data showing downregulation of sensory genes and reversibility of the injury state.

claim: Single cell sequencing has vastly expanded the definition of neural class.
source: Single cell sequencing has vastly expanded the definition of neural class, with the general assumption that distinct transcriptomic classes are fundamentally different types of cell (Li et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017; Tasic et al., 2018; Usoskin et al., 2015; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple single-cell sequencing studies.

claim: sn-sequencing defined a dozen new types of large diameter trigeminal neurons.
source: Here, sn-sequencing defined a dozen new types of large diameter trigeminal neurons (Supplementary file 2) that may have select functions in various types of mechanosensitive response.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The transcriptomic diversity that defines 27 distinct classes of uninjured trigeminal neurons is almost completely lost within 2 days of nerve injury.
source: Notably, however, we also demonstrated that the transcriptomic diversity that defines 27 distinct classes of uninjured trigeminal neurons is almost completely lost within 2 days of nerve injury.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transformation of diverse neurons into I1 and I2 classes shown in Figure 2.

claim: Relatively minor peripheral injury triggers the abrupt transcriptomic transition to an injured state.
source: This would be remarkable enough if the transformation required gross neural damage but is all the more so because relatively minor peripheral injury also triggers this abrupt transition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data from minor injury models shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Different transcriptomic classes can all be rapidly transformed to a much more uniform state and then reappear on recovery from injury.
source: However, the simple fact that the different transcriptomic classes can all be rapidly transformed to a much more uniform state (and then reappear on recovery from injury) exposes great transcriptional plasticity amongst somatosensory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transformation to I1/I2 and recovery data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: In the IOT experimental model, the injury-related gene expression program is essentially complete two days after injury and thus precedes the peak development of pain.
source: Here we demonstrate that in this experimental model the injury-related gene expression program is essentially complete two days after IOT and thus precedes the peak development of pain (Cobos et al., 2018; Hardt et al., 2019; Wlaschin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transcriptomic data at day 2 shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations about pain development timing.

claim: Neuropathic pain and mechanical allodynia primarily involves modulation of central processing rather than altered sensory input.
source: Thus, it is likely that symptoms are induced well downstream of gene-regulation in injured cells in keeping with recent studies suggesting that neuropathic pain and mechanical allodynia primarily involves modulation of central processing rather than altered sensory input (Guan et al., 2016; Szczot et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of transcriptomic changes versus pain development and supported by citations.

claim: Uninjured neurons are unchanged at a transcriptomic level after SNI.
source: Further support for this comes from the fact that uninjured neurons are unchanged at a transcriptomic level after SNI.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clustering analysis showing uninjured neurons maintain their normal profiles after IOT.

claim: Long-term peripheral trauma and delayed recovery might have some potential to trigger similar types of neuropathy to more frank nerve injury.
source: It is interesting that more minor injuries can induce a very similar pattern of gene expression, raising the possibility that long-term peripheral trauma and delayed recovery might have some potential to trigger similar types of neuropathy to more frank nerve injury.
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarity of gene expression changes across injury types.

claim: The type of nerve damage caused by transection makes it unlikely that precise reinnervation of target sites can be required for neurons to initiate the transition back to normal function.
source: Finally, we note that the type of nerve damage caused by transection makes it unlikely that precise reinnervation of target sites can be required for neurons to initiate the transition back to normal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of the injury and the observation of recovery.

claim: Aberrant signaling from neurons with inappropriate peripheral endings could contribute to some types of pain and sensory disturbances associated with severe injuries.
source: Indeed, it is possible that aberrant signaling from neurons with inappropriate peripheral endings could contribute to some types of pain and sensory disturbances associated with severe injuries.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of pain after severe injury.
